newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK base rates seen steady until January.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK base rates seen steady until January.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will almost certainly leave interest rates steady at 6.0 percent at his monetary meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday, a Reuters survey showed.
All 21 economists contacted by Reuters said they expected no rate move at the meeting.

They said their view had been reinforced by George's comments on Thursday to the House of Commons Treasury Select Committee. George said Clarke was "up with the game" when he raised rates 25 basis points to 6.0 percent in October.

One of the economists, Philip Shaw of Union Discount, originally forecast a 25-basis point rise at the meeting. But he altered his view following the ruling Conservative party's effective loss of a majority in parliament on Friday.

"The political situation is a lot more volatile now, given the Conservatives' perilous state in the House of Commons," Shaw said on Monday. "They may feel it is politically inappropriate to tighten monetary policy at this point."

Conservative member Sir John Gorst withdrew his support to the party on Friday in protest over a hospital closure in his north London constituency, capping what analysts said was Prime Minister John Major's worst week in power.
Economists said George's comments, combined with a fiscally tight budget, had let Clarke off the hook in December.

"The budget made a rate rise less likely and now that Eddie George has said he sees the budget as having a contractionary effect so the fact that the Bank isn't pushing so hard, makes it easier for Clarke," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at Societe Generale.
However, many economists warned that Clarke and George could yet deliver a surprise move, catching the markets out as they did on October 30 when they raised rates against expectations.
Since most analysts expect a rise in January or February, a move in December could have the advantage of getting the bad news on rates out of the way before the next general election.
Eighteen of the 21 economists predicted Clarke would have to raise rates by an average of 25 basis points before the general election, which must be held by May 22.

Late January or early February seemed likely, allowing Clarke to digest Christmas retail sales figures and a preliminary estimate for fourth quarter gross domestic product and avoid bad publicity just before the holiday season, economists said.
"He's a politician and the headlines wouldn't read very well -- "Mortgage rates up, Happy Christmas, love Ken Clarke,'" said Geoffrey Dicks, economist at Natwest Markets.
Mixed economic data would also permit Clarke to wait until the new year before making any policy changes.

"The chancellor will argue that with the recovery and manufacturing activity not yet assured, sterling's strength and pipeline pressures still very weak indeed...there's sufficient ambiguity in the data to justify a "wait-and-see' approach over this month," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
A November survey from the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) released on Thursday showed a slowdown in retail trade, with severe competition among retailers keeping a lid on prices.
"The CBI survey was not as bullish as the more excessive inflation hawks in the City had been suggesting," said James Stewart, chief economist at SE-Banken.
"I think the chancellor is quite right to err on the side of caution. He would be justified in waiting and he might sanction another 25 basis points in February," added Stewart.
